solution:
\(f\) is a polynomial, so it is defined for every real \(x\) and its limit at any point equals its value there.
\(f(-2) = (-2)^{3} + 2(-2)^{2} - (-2) - 2 = -8 + 8 + 2 - 2 = 0\).
\(\lim_{x \to -2} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -2} (x^{3} + 2x^{2} - x - 2) = 0 = f(-2)\).
All three conditions hold, so \(f\) is continuous at \(x = -2\).

Since \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) satisfies \(x \le \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
Left limit: \(\lim_{x \to \pi/4^{-}} \sin x = \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
Right limit: \(\lim_{x \to \pi/4^{+}} \cos x = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
The two one-sided limits agree, so the limit exists and equals the value of the function.
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

\(f(3) = 8\) (given).
For \(x \ne 3\), \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^{2} - 9}{x - 3} = \dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{x - 3} = x + 3\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = 3 + 3 = 6\).
The limit exists but \(6 \ne 8 = f(3)\), so the third condition fails.
\(\therefore f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 3\), and the discontinuity is removable (redefining \(f(3) = 6\) would make it continuous).

\(x = 2\) satisfies \(x \le 2\), so \(f(2) = 2^{3} - 2(2) + 1 = 8 - 4 + 1 = 5\).
Left limit: \(\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} (x^{3} - 2x + 1) = 5\).
Right limit: \(\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} (3x - 2) = 6 - 2 = 4\).
Since \(5 \ne 4\), the two one-sided limits differ, so \(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\) does not exist.
\(\therefore f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 2\) (a jump discontinuity).

\(x = 0\) satisfies \(x \ge 0\), so \(f(0) = \dfrac{7}{3}\), and the right limit is also \(\dfrac{7}{3}\).
Left limit: \(\lim_{x \to 0^{-}} \left( \dfrac{x}{\tan 3x} + 2 \right) = \lim_{x \to 0^{-}} \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{3x}{\tan 3x} + 2 = \dfrac{1}{3}(1) + 2 = \dfrac{7}{3}\), using \(\lim_{\theta \to 0} \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\theta} = 1\).
Both one-sided limits equal \(\dfrac{7}{3} = f(0)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).

\(f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor\) is constant on each interval between consecutive integers, so it can only break at integers. The integers lying in \((-3, 2)\) are \(-2, -1, 0, 1\).
At any such integer \(n\): \(\lim_{x \to n^{-}} \lfloor x \rfloor = n - 1\) while \(\lim_{x \to n^{+}} \lfloor x \rfloor = n = f(n)\), so the one-sided limits differ and \(\lim_{x \to n} f(x)\) does not exist.
For example at \(x = 0\): left limit \(= -1\), right limit \(= 0\).
\(\therefore f\) is discontinuous at \(x = -2,\ x = -1,\ x = 0,\ x = 1\) (jump discontinuities), and continuous at every other point of \((-3, 2)\).

\(f\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = \left| 2\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) + 3 \right| = |0| = 0\).
For \(x < -\dfrac{3}{2}\), \(2x + 3 < 0\), so \(f(x) = -(2x + 3)\) and \(\lim_{x \to -3/2^{-}} f(x) = 0\).
For \(x > -\dfrac{3}{2}\), \(2x + 3 > 0\), so \(f(x) = 2x + 3\) and \(\lim_{x \to -3/2^{+}} f(x) = 0\).
Both one-sided limits equal \(0 = f\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = -\dfrac{3}{2}\).

\(f(2) = \dfrac{1}{5}\) (given). Put \(t = x - 1\), so \(x - 2 = t - 1\) and \(t \to 1\) as \(x \to 2\).
\(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \lim_{t \to 1} \dfrac{t^{1/2} - t^{1/3}}{t - 1} = \lim_{t \to 1} \dfrac{t^{1/2} - 1}{t - 1} - \lim_{t \to 1} \dfrac{t^{1/3} - 1}{t - 1}\).
Using \(\lim_{t \to a} \dfrac{t^{n} - a^{n}}{t - a} = n a^{n-1}\) with \(a = 1\), these are \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{3}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{6}\).
The limit exists but \(\dfrac{1}{6} \ne \dfrac{1}{5} = f(2)\).
\(\therefore f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 2\) (removable discontinuity).

\(f(2) = -24\) (given). For \(x \ne 2\), multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(\sqrt{x + 2} + \sqrt{3x - 2}\):
\(f(x) = \dfrac{(x^{3} - 8)\left( \sqrt{x + 2} + \sqrt{3x - 2} \right)}{(x + 2) - (3x - 2)} = \dfrac{(x - 2)(x^{2} + 2x + 4)\left( \sqrt{x + 2} + \sqrt{3x - 2} \right)}{-2(x - 2)}\).
Cancelling \(x - 2\) and letting \(x \to 2\):
\(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \dfrac{(4 + 4 + 4)(2 + 2)}{-2} = \dfrac{48}{-2} = -24 = f(2)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\).

\(x = \dfrac{8}{3}\) satisfies \(x \le \dfrac{8}{3}\), so \(f\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) = 4\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) + 1 = \dfrac{35}{3}\).
Left limit: \(\lim_{x \to 8/3^{-}} (4x + 1) = \dfrac{35}{3}\).
Right limit: \(\lim_{x \to 8/3^{+}} \dfrac{59 - 9x}{3} = \dfrac{59 - 24}{3} = \dfrac{35}{3}\).
Both one-sided limits equal the value of the function.
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = \dfrac{8}{3}\).

\(f(0) = 2\) (given). For \(x \ne 0\), write both roots about their values at \(x = 0\):
Numerator \(= 3\left[ \left(1 - \dfrac{2x}{27}\right)^{1/3} - 1 \right]\) and denominator \(= 9\left[ 1 - \left(1 + \dfrac{5x}{243}\right)^{1/5} \right]\).
Using \(\lim_{u \to 0} \dfrac{(1 + u)^{n} - 1}{u} = n\):
Numerator \(\approx 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\left(-\dfrac{2x}{27}\right) = -\dfrac{2x}{27}\), denominator \(\approx -9 \cdot \dfrac{1}{5}\left(\dfrac{5x}{243}\right) = -\dfrac{x}{27}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \dfrac{-2x/27}{-x/27} = 2 = f(0)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).

\(f(2) = 12\) (given). Near \(x = 2\) only the first branch applies, since \(2 \in (0, 3)\).
\(x^{2} + 8x - 20 = (x + 10)(x - 2)\) and \(2x^{2} - 9x + 10 = (2x - 5)(x - 2)\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2} \dfrac{x + 10}{2x - 5} = \dfrac{12}{-1} = -12\).
The limit exists but \(-12 \ne 12 = f(2)\).
\(\therefore f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 2\) (removable discontinuity).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = 7\), so it is discontinuous there.
For \(x \ne 7\), \(f(x) = \dfrac{(x - 3)(x - 7)}{x - 7} = x - 3\), so \(\lim_{x \to 7} f(x) = 4\).
The limit exists and is finite, only the value is missing, so the gap can be closed by defining \(f(7) = 4\).
\(\therefore\) the discontinuity at \(x = 7\) is removable.

Each branch is a polynomial, so the only possible break is at \(x = 4\).
\(f(4) = 16 + 12 - 2 = 26\); left limit \(= \lim_{x \to 4^{-}} (x^{2} + 3x - 2) = 26\).
Right limit \(= \lim_{x \to 4^{+}} (5x + 3) = 23\).
The one-sided limits are finite but unequal \((26 \ne 23)\), so the limit does not exist and no redefinition of \(f(4)\) can help.
\(\therefore f\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x = 4\), of jump \(23 - 26 = -3\).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = -3\) (neither branch includes it), so that is the only doubtful point.
Left limit \(= \lim_{x \to -3^{-}} (x^{2} - 3x - 2) = 9 + 9 - 2 = 16\).
Right limit \(= \lim_{x \to -3^{+}} (3 + 8x) = 3 - 24 = -21\).
The one-sided limits are finite but unequal, so \(\lim_{x \to -3} f(x)\) does not exist.
\(\therefore f\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x = -3\), of jump \(-21 - 16 = -37\).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = \pi\).
Left limit \(= \lim_{x \to \pi^{-}} (4 + \sin x) = 4 + 0 = 4\).
Right limit \(= \lim_{x \to \pi^{+}} (3 - \cos x) = 3 - (-1) = 4\).
The two agree, so \(\lim_{x \to \pi} f(x) = 4\) exists; only the value at \(x = \pi\) is missing.
\(\therefore\) the discontinuity at \(x = \pi\) is removable (define \(f(\pi) = 4\)).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = 0\), since \(\sin 0 = 0\).
Using \(1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^{2} x\), for \(x \ne 0\) near \(0\): \(f(x) = \dfrac{2\sin^{2} x}{\sin x} = 2\sin x\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 2\sin 0 = 0\), a finite limit, so a continuous extension exists.
The continuous extension is obtained by defining \(f(0) = 0\).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = 0\), since \(1 - \cos^{2} x = \sin^{2} x = 0\) there.
Using \(1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^{2} x\) and \(1 - \cos^{2} x = \sin^{2} x\), for \(x \ne 0\):
\(f(x) = \dfrac{3\sin^{2} x + 4\sin^{2} x \cos x}{2\sin^{2} x} = \dfrac{3 + 4\cos x}{2}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \dfrac{3 + 4}{2} = \dfrac{7}{2}\), a finite limit, so a continuous extension exists.
The continuous extension is obtained by defining \(f(0) = \dfrac{7}{2}\).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = -1\), since \(x^{3} + 1 = 0\) there.
For \(x \ne -1\): \(f(x) = \dfrac{(x - 1)(x + 1)}{(x + 1)(x^{2} - x + 1)} = \dfrac{x - 1}{x^{2} - x + 1}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to -1} f(x) = \dfrac{-2}{1 + 1 + 1} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\), a finite limit, so a continuous extension exists.
The continuous extension is obtained by defining \(f(-1) = -\dfrac{2}{3}\).

\(f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{3}{4}\) (given). Put \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + h\), so \(h \to 0\) and \(\pi - 3x = -3h\).
\(\sqrt{3} - \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + h\right) = \sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + \tan h}{1 - \sqrt{3}\tan h} = \dfrac{-4\tan h}{1 - \sqrt{3}\tan h}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to \pi/3} f(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{-4\tan h}{-3h\left(1 - \sqrt{3}\tan h\right)} = \dfrac{4}{3} \cdot 1 = \dfrac{4}{3}\).
The limit exists but \(\dfrac{4}{3} \ne \dfrac{3}{4} = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\).
\(\therefore f\) is discontinuous at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (removable discontinuity).

\(f(0) = 1\) (given).
As \(x \to 0^{+}\), \(\dfrac{1}{x} \to +\infty\) so \(e^{1/x} \to \infty\). Dividing above and below by \(e^{1/x}\): \(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \dfrac{1 - e^{-1/x}}{1 + e^{-1/x}} = \dfrac{1 - 0}{1 + 0} = 1\).
As \(x \to 0^{-}\), \(\dfrac{1}{x} \to -\infty\) so \(e^{1/x} \to 0\), giving \(\lim_{x \to 0^{-}} f(x) = \dfrac{0 - 1}{0 + 1} = -1\).
Since \(1 \ne -1\), \(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\) does not exist.
\(\therefore f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 0\) (an irremovable jump discontinuity).

\(f(0) = \dfrac{(\log 2)^{2}}{2}\) (given).
Numerator \(= \left(2^{x}\right)^{2} - 2 \cdot 2^{x} + 1 = \left(2^{x} - 1\right)^{2}\); denominator \(= 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^{2} x\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{1}{2}\left( \dfrac{2^{x} - 1}{x} \right)^{2} \left( \dfrac{x}{\sin x} \right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}(\log 2)^{2}(1)^{2} = \dfrac{(\log 2)^{2}}{2}\).
This equals \(f(0)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).

\(f(0) = \dfrac{3}{4}\) (given). Divide numerator and denominator by \(x\):
Numerator: \(\dfrac{e^{5\sin x} - 1}{x} - \dfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{x} = 5 \cdot \dfrac{e^{5\sin x} - 1}{5\sin x} \cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{x} - 2 \cdot \dfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{2x} \to 5 - 2 = 3\).
Denominator: \(\dfrac{5\tan x - 3x}{x} = 5 \cdot \dfrac{\tan x}{x} - 3 \to 5 - 3 = 2\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}\), which exists but differs from \(f(0) = \dfrac{3}{4}\).
The discontinuity is removable; redefining \(f(0) = \dfrac{3}{2}\) makes \(f\) continuous at \(x = 0\).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = 0\).
Right limit: \(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \dfrac{\log(1 + 5x)}{\log(1 + 3x)} = \lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \dfrac{5 \cdot \dfrac{\log(1 + 5x)}{5x}}{3 \cdot \dfrac{\log(1 + 3x)}{3x}} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).
Left limit: \(\lim_{x \to 0^{-}} \dfrac{32^{x} - 1}{8^{x} - 1} = \dfrac{\log 32}{\log 8} = \dfrac{5\log 2}{3\log 2} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).
Both one-sided limits are \(\dfrac{5}{3}\), so \(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \dfrac{5}{3}\) exists while \(f(0)\) is undefined.
The discontinuity is removable; defining \(f(0) = \dfrac{5}{3}\) makes \(f\) continuous at \(x = 0\).

\(f\) is not defined at \(x = 0\). As \(x \to 0\) the base \(\to 1\) and the index \(\to \infty\), an \(1^{\infty}\) form.
Base \(- 1 = \dfrac{3 - 8x}{3 - 2x} - 1 = \dfrac{-6x}{3 - 2x}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = e^{\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{-6x}{3 - 2x}} = e^{-6/3} = e^{-2}\).
The limit exists and is finite while \(f(0)\) is undefined.
The discontinuity is removable; defining \(f(0) = e^{-2}\) makes \(f\) continuous at \(x = 0\).

Each branch is a polynomial, so the only doubtful point is \(x = -2\).
\(f(-2) = 3(-2) + 2 = -4\); left limit \(= \lim_{x \to -2^{-}} (3x + 2) = -4\).
Right limit \(= \lim_{x \to -2^{+}} (2x - 3) = -4 - 3 = -7\).
Since \(-4 \ne -7\), the limit does not exist, and no choice of \(f(-2)\) can repair that.
\(\therefore f\) has an irremovable (jump) discontinuity at \(x = -2\); it cannot be redefined to become continuous.

\(f(2) = 3\) (given).
Right limit: \(\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} \dfrac{(x - 2)(x^{2} + 2x + 4)}{(x - 2)(x + 2)} = \dfrac{4 + 4 + 4}{4} = 3\).
Left limit: put \(t = 3(x - 2)^{2} \to 0\), then \(\dfrac{e^{t} - 1}{2(x - 2)^{2}} = \dfrac{e^{t} - 1}{t} \cdot \dfrac{3(x - 2)^{2}}{2(x - 2)^{2}} \to 1 \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\).
Since \(\dfrac{3}{2} \ne 3\), the one-sided limits differ and \(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\) does not exist.
\(\therefore f\) has an irremovable (jump) discontinuity at \(x = 2\); it cannot be redefined to become continuous.

For continuity at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) we need \(f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \lim_{x \to \pi/2} f(x)\).
Multiplying by the conjugate \(\sqrt{2 + \sin x} + \sqrt{3}\) and using \(\cos^{2} x = 1 - \sin^{2} x\):
\(f(x) = \dfrac{\sin x - 1}{(1 - \sin x)(1 + \sin x)\left( \sqrt{2 + \sin x} + \sqrt{3} \right)} = \dfrac{-1}{(1 + \sin x)\left( \sqrt{2 + \sin x} + \sqrt{3} \right)}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to \pi/2} f(x) = \dfrac{-1}{(1 + 1)\left( \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{3} \right)} = \dfrac{-1}{4\sqrt{3}}\).
\(\therefore f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{3}}\).

For continuity at \(x = 0\) we need \(f(0) = \lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\).
Numerator \(= \cos 2x - 1 = -2\sin^{2} x\); rationalising the denominator, \(\sqrt{3x^{2} + 1} - 1 = \dfrac{3x^{2}}{\sqrt{3x^{2} + 1} + 1}\).
\(\therefore f(x) = \dfrac{-2\sin^{2} x \left( \sqrt{3x^{2} + 1} + 1 \right)}{3x^{2}} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\left( \dfrac{\sin x}{x} \right)^{2}\left( \sqrt{3x^{2} + 1} + 1 \right)\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = -\dfrac{2}{3}(1)^{2}(1 + 1) = -\dfrac{4}{3}\).
\(\therefore f(0) = -\dfrac{4}{3}\).

For continuity at \(x = \pi\) we need \(f(\pi) = \lim_{x \to \pi} f(x)\). Put \(t = x - \pi \to 0\).
\(4^{t} + 4^{-t} - 2 = \left( 2^{t} - 2^{-t} \right)^{2}\), so \(f = \left( \dfrac{2^{t} - 2^{-t}}{t} \right)^{2}\).
Now \(\dfrac{2^{t} - 2^{-t}}{t} = \dfrac{2^{t} - 1}{t} + \dfrac{2^{-t} - 1}{-t} \to \log 2 + \log 2 = 2\log 2\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to \pi} f(x) = (2\log 2)^{2} = 4(\log 2)^{2}\).
\(\therefore f(\pi) = 4(\log 2)^{2}\).

Factorise both by grouping:
Numerator \(= 8^{x}3^{x} - 8^{x} - 3^{x} + 1 = \left( 8^{x} - 1 \right)\left( 3^{x} - 1 \right)\).
Denominator \(= 4^{x}3^{x} - 4^{x} - 3^{x} + 1 = \left( 4^{x} - 1 \right)\left( 3^{x} - 1 \right)\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left( 8^{x} - 1 \right)/x}{\left( 4^{x} - 1 \right)/x} = \dfrac{\log 8}{\log 4} = \dfrac{3\log 2}{2\log 2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\).
For continuity at \(x = 0\), \(k = \lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\).
\(\therefore k = \dfrac{3}{2}\).

\(5^{x} + 5^{-x} - 2 = \left( 5^{x} - 1 \right)\left( 1 - 5^{-x} \right)\), since expanding gives \(5^{x} - 1 - 1 + 5^{-x}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{5^{x} - 1}{x} \cdot \dfrac{1 - 5^{-x}}{x} = \log 5 \cdot \log 5 = (\log 5)^{2}\),
using \(\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{5^{-x} - 1}{-x} = \log 5\).
For continuity at \(x = 0\), \(k = \lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\).
\(\therefore k = (\log 5)^{2}\).

\(f(0) = 4\). For continuity at \(x = 0\) both one-sided limits must equal \(4\).
Right limit: \(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \left( \dfrac{\sin 2x}{5x} - a \right) = \dfrac{2}{5}\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \dfrac{\sin 2x}{2x} - a = \dfrac{2}{5} - a\).
\(\dfrac{2}{5} - a = 4 \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{2}{5} - 4 = -\dfrac{18}{5}\).
Left limit: \(\lim_{x \to 0^{-}} \left( x^{2} + b - 3 \right) = b - 3\), and \(b - 3 = 4 \Rightarrow b = 7\).
\(\therefore a = -\dfrac{18}{5},\ b = 7\).

Each branch is a polynomial, so continuity can only fail at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\).
At \(x = 0\): \(f(0) = 2b + 18\) and \(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} f(x) = 3a - b\), so \(2b + 18 = 3a - b\), i.e. \(a - b = 6\).
At \(x = 2\): \(f(2) = 4 + 3a - b\) and \(\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = 16 - 2 = 14\), so \(3a - b = 10\).
Substituting \(b = a - 6\) into \(3a - b = 10\): \(3a - a + 6 = 10 \Rightarrow a = 2\), hence \(b = -4\).
\(\therefore a = 2,\ b = -4\).

The only doubtful points are \(x = 2\) and \(x = 3\).
At \(x = 2\): \(\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} \dfrac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{x - 2} = 4\) and \(f(2) = 4a - 2b + 3\), so \(4a - 2b + 3 = 4\), i.e. \(4a - 2b = 1\).
At \(x = 3\): \(\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} \left( ax^{2} - bx + 3 \right) = 9a - 3b + 3\) and \(f(3) = 6 - a + b\), so \(9a - 3b + 3 = 6 - a + b\), i.e. \(10a - 4b = 3\).
Doubling the first gives \(8a - 4b = 2\); subtracting from \(10a - 4b = 3\) gives \(2a = 1\), so \(a = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and then \(2 - 2b = 1\) gives \(b = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
\(\therefore a = \dfrac{1}{2},\ b = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

The domain is \([-3, 7]\). Modulus functions are continuous everywhere, so \(f\) is continuous on \([-3, 2)\) and on \((2, 7]\); only \(x = 2\) needs checking.
\(f(2) = |2 + 1| = 3\) and \(\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} |x + 1| = 3\).
\(\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} |x - 5| = |2 - 5| = 3\).
All three are equal, so \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\) as well.
\(\therefore f\) is continuous on its whole domain \([-3, 7]\).

\(f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\) (given). Put \(t = 1 + \sin 2x\); then \((\sin x + \cos x)^{2} = 1 + \sin 2x = t\), so \((\sin x + \cos x)^{3} = t^{3/2}\) and \(\sin 2x - 1 = t - 2\).
As \(x \to \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(\sin 2x \to 1\) so \(t \to 2\), and \(2\sqrt{2} = 2^{3/2}\).
\(\therefore \lim_{x \to \pi/4} f(x) = \lim_{t \to 2} \dfrac{t^{3/2} - 2^{3/2}}{t - 2} = \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot 2^{1/2} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\), using \(\lim_{t \to a} \dfrac{t^{n} - a^{n}}{t - a} = n a^{n-1}\).
This equals \(f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

\(|x - 2| \ge 1\) means \(x \le 1\) or \(x \ge 3\), so \(f(x) = x^{2} + px + q\) there and \(f(x) = x + 1\) on \((1, 3)\). Each piece is a polynomial, so only \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\) need checking.
At \(x = 1\): \(f(1) = 1 + p + q\) and \(\lim_{x \to 1^{+}} (x + 1) = 2\), so \(1 + p + q = 2\), i.e. \(p + q = 1\).
At \(x = 3\): \(\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} (x + 1) = 4\) and \(f(3) = 9 + 3p + q\), so \(9 + 3p + q = 4\), i.e. \(3p + q = -5\).
Subtracting, \(2p = -6\), so \(p = -3\) and \(q = 1 - p = 4\).
\(\therefore p = -3,\ q = 4\).

Let \(f(x) = 2x^{3} - x - 16\). Being a polynomial, \(f\) is continuous on \([2, 3]\).
\(f(2) = 2(8) - 2 - 16 = -2 < 0\).
\(f(3) = 2(27) - 3 - 16 = 35 > 0\).
So \(f(2)\) and \(f(3)\) have opposite signs, and \(0\) lies between \(f(2)\) and \(f(3)\).
By the Intermediate Value Theorem there exists \(c \in (2, 3)\) with \(f(c) = 0\).
\(\therefore\) the equation \(2x^{3} - x - 16 = 0\) has a root between \(2\) and \(3\).

Let \(f(x) = x^{3} - 3x\). Being a polynomial, \(f\) is continuous on \([1, 2]\).
\(f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2 < 0\).
\(f(2) = 8 - 6 = 2 > 0\).
So \(f(1)\) and \(f(2)\) have opposite signs, and \(0\) lies between them.
By the Intermediate Value Theorem there exists \(c \in (1, 2)\) with \(f(c) = 0\).
\(\therefore\) the equation \(x^{3} - 3x = 0\) has a root between \(1\) and \(2\) (in fact \(c = \sqrt{3}\)).

The stem prints no interval against either branch, so as written both formulas would apply on all of \(\mathbb{R}\). Fig. 8.11 settles the intent: the parabola \(y = x^{2} + 5\) is drawn only for \(x \ge 1\), with a solid dot at \((1, 6)\) and nothing to its left, so the linear piece is meant for \(x < 1\):
\(f(x) = ax + b\) for \(x < 1\), \(f(x) = x^{2} + 5\) for \(x \ge 1\).
Then \(f(1) = 1 + 5 = 6\) and \(\lim_{x \to 1^{+}} f(x) = 6\), while \(\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} f(x) = a + b\).
Continuity at \(x = 1\) therefore requires only \(a + b = 6\).
That is ONE equation in TWO unknowns, so \(a\) and \(b\) are not determined individually: every pair with \(a + b = 6\) works, for instance \(a = 1,\ b = 5\) or \(a = 6,\ b = 0\).
\(\therefore\) the required condition is \(a + b = 6\); the question as printed is under-determined and fixes no unique \(a\) and \(b\).
_note: Under-determined as printed, and the book prints no answer for Q17. Continuity at x = 1 gives only a + b = 6. Reported as the condition rather than inventing a second equation to pin a and b down.

solution:
Each piece is a polynomial, so \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b)\) and on \((b, c]\); only \(x = b\) needs checking. Since \(b\) lies in the first piece:
\(f(b) = pb + 3\).
\(\lim_{x \to b^{+}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to b^{+}} \left( 5x^{2} - q \right) = 5b^{2} - q\).
For continuity at \(x = b\) these must be equal:
\(\therefore pb + 3 = 5b^{2} - q\).
\(\therefore pb = 5b^{2} - q - 3\), so \(p = \dfrac{5b^{2} - q - 3}{b}\) is the required condition (with \(b \ne 0\)).
